newsitem.title: USA: WEEK AHEAD-Wall Street to get read on earnings.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Wall Street to get read on earnings.

text.p: With the corporate earnings season heating up this week, Wall Street will get a key signal of whether stock prices are overblown after racking up their biggest quarterly gain in 10 years.
The speculation is that if second-quarter earnings prove to be as good as many analysts expect, then the bull market will be intact, perhaps up to the end of the year.

Stocks have been barrelling higher and in the last three months the Dow Jones industrial average has gained an eye-popping 1,225 points, or 19 percent, the largest advance since March 1987, when it soared nearly 22 percent.

After a holiday-shortened trading week, the Dow closed Thursday with a gain of 100.43 points at a new high of 7,895.81, eclipsing its June 20 record finish of 7,796.51. For the week it was up 208.09 points.
The market's ascent has been fuelled by a near-perfect scenario of steady earnings growth and an economy that shows no signs of generating inflation.
Another addition to the cheery scenario is Washington's deal to balance the federal budget, which could eventually bring lower interest rates.
Despite the positive atmosphere, stocks are still vulnerable to the quarterly earnings test, and investors will get their first taste of corporate results in the coming week.
A sampling of analysts' estimates shows that second-quarter profits will be positive and most of the bad news or so-called earnings surprises have already been pre-announced.

First Call, a Boston-based firm that tracks analysts' earnings forecasts, said the Standard and Poor's 500 companies are expected to report a 9.1 percent rise in second-quarter operating profits, compared with a gain in the first quarter of 15.1 percent.
But the company noted that analysts typically low-ball the earnings numbers by an average of 2.6 percent and the total will likely be adjusted higher.

"If we follow the normal pattern of the last three years, and given the normal negative pre-announcements, we should expect to get the usual positive bias," said Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call.
"When all the reporting is done, we should get something approaching 12 percent earnings gain over last year," he said.

Al Kugel, senior investment strategist for Stein Roe & Farnham, a Chicago-based mutual fund, said the market will stay on an upward course in the second half of the year, although the gain may not be as "sensational" as in the last three months.
"We are going into the second quarter with a strong market that is already anticipating good results, and it may be hard to get the same upward lift again," he said.
Kugel said that mutual fund investors are buying stocks for their long-term earnings prospects, and the positive outlook for the economy and inflation should keep the market sizzling.
But others warned that the fastest market gains are often the quickest to evaporate.
Michael Metz, of Oppenheimer & Co, and a long-time Wall Street bear, views the earnings story differently and says now is not the time for heroes.

"Earnings will not get better in the second half of the year and I think we've passed the peak earnings period after corporations have been able to expand their profit margins, particularly in the second quarter," he said.
